title: The filter shape: empty list, loop, append
idea: TOOL: the concrete filter pattern — make an empty list, loop, test with if, append the passers. Shown with predictable output.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

scores = [4, 9, 2, 7]
kept = []
for score in scores:
    if score > 5:
        kept.append(score)
print(kept)
exercises.explanation: Each score is tested with score > 5. Only 9 and 7 pass and get appended, so kept ends up [9, 7].

exercises.prompt: Why does the filter start with kept = [] (an empty list)?
options: So there is somewhere to collect the items that pass
Because the original list must be empty
It is just decoration and does nothing
exercises.explanation: You need an empty basket before you start picking. Each passing item gets appended into kept.

exercises.prompt: The append happens INSIDE the if, so only items that pass the test are added.
exercises.explanation: The append is indented under the if. It only runs when the condition is true, so only passers are kept.
append adds the item to the end of the list. You met it earlier — here it collects each number that passes n < 10.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

nums = [12, 3, 20, 8]
kept = []
for n in nums:
    if n < 10:
        kept.append(n)
print(kept)
exercises.explanation: Only 3 and 8 are below 10, so they are appended in the order they appear: [3, 8].

exercises.prompt: Arrange these lines into a working filter that keeps scores above 5.
exercises.explanation: List first, empty kept list, then the loop with the test, the append inside the if, and finally print the result.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

ages = [15, 22, 8, 40]
adults = []
for age in ages:
    if age >= 18:
        adults.append(age)
print(adults)
exercises.explanation: age >= 18 keeps only 22 and 40. The others are younger and left out, so adults is [22, 40].

exercises.prompt: If you forget the kept = [] line before the loop, the program has no list to append into.
exercises.explanation: The empty list must exist before the loop starts appending. Without it, there is nowhere to collect the passers.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

prices = [3, 8, 1, 6]
cheap = []
for price in prices:
    if price <= 5:
        cheap.append(price)
print(cheap)
exercises.explanation: price <= 5 passes for 3 and 1 only. They are appended in order, giving [3, 1].
'10 or more' means greater-than-or-equal, so the comparison is >=. You saw this comparison back in the booleans unit.
